articles.headline: More Women Are Taking Hormone Therapy. Here's What Changed.
articles.body: For years, hormone therapy prescriptions were the exception. Now they're becoming the norm. Data from 2026 shows estrogen-based HRT prescribing more than doubled from 2018 to 2026, with the biggest surges in patches and vaginal creams. Among women aged 45-54, one in 20 now has an HRT prescription. What sparked the shift? A better understanding of timing. Modern research shows hormone therapy works differently depending on when you start—beginning close to menopause onset has a more favorable risk-benefit profile than years after. This evolution reflects decades of new science beyond the old headlines that scared millions of women away from treatment.
articles.takeaway: If menopause symptoms are disrupting your life, talk to your doctor about timing and route of delivery. The science has evolved considerably from what you may have heard 20 years ago.

articles.headline: The Ice Chamber That's Becoming Real Sports Recovery.
articles.body: Whole-body cryotherapy—extreme cold exposure at minus 110 to minus 160 degrees Celsius—sounds brutal. But a new meta-analysis published in Nature's Scientific Reports shows it actually reduces inflammatory markers in your blood. The research reviewed 11 randomized controlled trials and found consistent reductions in inflammation and pain, making it genuinely useful for athletes recovering from hard training. The mechanism is straightforward: extreme cold triggers your sympathetic nervous system, releasing noradrenaline and shifting your immune response from inflammation to repair. Most sessions last just 2 to 3 minutes. The evidence is strongest for post-exercise recovery and chronic inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis.
articles.takeaway: If you're training hard and inflammation is slowing your recovery, cryotherapy has real science behind it. Ice baths work too, but WBC is faster if you have access.

articles.headline: Your Flexibility Score May Predict How Long You Live.
articles.body: A 13-year study of 3,139 adults ages 46 to 65 found something striking: greater flexibility was linked with a lower risk of premature death. Men with low flexibility scores were almost twice as likely to die during the study compared to those with higher scores. This isn't about yoga vanity—it's about mobility preserving your ability to stay active and independent. The researchers measured range of motion at seven joint sites: ankles, shoulders, knees, spine, wrists, hips and elbows. The payoff? Increased flexibility improves your ability to move without pain, which keeps you exercising, which keeps you healthier. It's a chain reaction that starts with how freely your joints can move.
articles.takeaway: Test your range of motion at your hips, shoulders and spine. If you're stiff, consistent mobility work may add years to your life.

articles.headline: Your Mental Toughness Just Became Your Best Stress Shield.
articles.body: A new study published in Frontiers in Psychology reveals that mental toughness genuinely moderates the damage stress does to your mental health. Researchers found that people with higher mental toughness showed lower rates of depression and anxiety when facing high stress compared to those with lower mental toughness. This matters because stress is inevitable. What changes is whether it crushes you or you bounce back. The study measured mental toughness as your capacity to cope with challenges, maintain focus under pressure, and recover emotionally. The good news: mental toughness isn't fixed. It builds through practice—facing hard things, pushing through discomfort, and consistently choosing forward momentum over defeat. Every difficult workout, every hard conversation, every challenge you complete strengthens this muscle.
articles.takeaway: Stress won't go away, but your ability to handle it can improve dramatically. Build mental toughness by regularly doing hard things.

quote.text: Resilient people do not bounce back from hard experiences; they find healthy ways to integrate them into their lives.
quote.author: Eric Greitens
quote.context: Former Navy SEAL and author on resilience and psychology

workout.title: Walk-Run Pyramid: Building the Base
workout.tip: Keep your shoulders relaxed and land with a midfoot strike. If you feel breathless during the running intervals, slow down by 0.5 mph—comfort over speed at this stage.
workout.warmup: 2 min @ 2.5 mph / 0% incline (easy walk) + 1 min @ 3.0 mph / 0% incline (brisk walk)

exercises.name: Walk-Run Interval Pyramid
exercises.notes: Execute the following sequence: 1 min walk @ 3.2 mph / 0% + 1 min run @ 5.0 mph / 0% → 1 min walk @ 3.2 mph / 0% + 2 min run @ 5.0 mph / 0% → 1 min walk @ 3.2 mph / 0% + 3 min run @ 5.0 mph / 0% → 1 min walk @ 3.2 mph / 0% + 2 min run @ 5.0 mph / 0% → 1 min walk @ 3.2 mph / 0% + 1 min run @ 5.0 mph / 0%. Focus on steady breathing and relaxed arm swing throughout all transitions.

workout.cooldown: 2 min @ 3.0 mph / 0% incline (easy walk). Post-run: hamstring stretch 30 sec each leg, quad stretch 30 sec each leg, calf stretch 20 sec each leg.
workout.description: A structured walk-run progression designed for complete beginners or runners returning from a long break. This session uses a pyramid format to build confidence and aerobic capacity without overload, perfect for establishing a sustainable treadmill routine before progressing to continuous running.

meal.title: Turkey Sandwich with Mustard & White Bread
meal.description: A simple, portable race-day fuel option for triathletes who prefer something savory. Easy to digest 2–3 hours before competition, with lean protein and quick carbs.
meal.instructions:
1. Spread mustard and honey evenly on two slices of bread.
2. Layer turkey slices between the bread.
3. Cut into triangles if desired for easier eating.
4. Eat 2–3 hours before race start with water on the side.
meal.tip: Buy pre-sliced turkey from the deli counter (not packaged) for better quality and less sodium if GI sensitivity is a concern. Store in a cool bag for morning transport.
